clue.text: Boy about to correct one's disloyalty

indicators.note: one word standing about others wraps around them, so the boy's word goes on the outside

parts.note: a boy is a son
to edit a text is to correct it
the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A boy is about to put right his own disloyal behaviour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About to' reads as 'on the point of', but 'about' is the wrapping signal and 'to correct' is one unit.
explanation.definitionFit: Sedition is speech or conduct inciting rebellion against the state, a form of disloyalty.

clue.text: Sorry, the piglets don't have nightmares!

indicators.note: something in a sorry state is in a mess, so the letters that follow are jumbled

parts.note: ten letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: An apology to the piglets, wishing them peaceful dreams.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sorry' reads as an apology to the piglets, but it is the signal to rearrange them.
explanation.definitionFit: The bedtime farewell 'sleep tight' is a wish that someone rests well, without bad dreams.

clue.text: Gear for one version of "London Calling"?

definitions.text: Gear for one version of "London Calling"?

parts.note: surface reading: a cover of the Clash song, or the BBC wartime call sign
setter's reading: the equipment a Londoner uses to call, named in Cockney rhyming slang

explanation.walkthrough: In Cockney rhyming slang, the dialect of London's East End, a phone is called by a phrase rhyming with it; this one is the 'London' version of the calling gear.
explanation.definitionFit: Dog and bone is rhyming slang for telephone, the device used for calling.

clue.text: Emotional start to the new year

indicators.note: a new version of a word is a fresh arrangement of its letters
the start of a word is its opening letter, so only that one is kept

parts.note: first letter of the
the four letters rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone feeling choked up as the new year begins.
explanation.definitionFit: Teary means close to tears, which describes someone emotional.

clue.text: The reason why money became my missed opportunity?

parts.words: The reason why money became my
parts.note: surface reading: a riddle about how someone's money turned into theirs
setter's reading: the letters of the word one escape from money, leaving my

explanation.surface: Someone muses on how money became theirs, and calls it a missed chance.
explanation.walkthrough: Take ONE away from MONEY and MY is left: ONE THAT GOT AWAY explains the change.
explanation.definitionFit: The one that got away is an idiom, from anglers' tales, for a prize or chance that slipped from one's grasp.

clue.text: Still difficult to sit in silence

indicators.note: something sitting in another thing is placed inside it

parts.note: the hushing sound demanding silence
a moot point is a debatable, difficult one

explanation.surface: It is still hard to sit in silence.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Still' looks like an adverb meaning 'even now', but it is the adjective for calm water.
explanation.definitionFit: Still water is smooth, with an undisturbed, unruffled surface.

clue.text: Vehicle fitted with ABS?

parts.note: surface reading: a car with an anti-lock braking system
setter's reading: abs as in abdominal muscles, so a vehicle with a toned body

explanation.walkthrough: ABS on a car means anti-lock brakes; read as abs, it means the six-pack muscles.
explanation.definitionFit: A muscle car is a powerful, high-performance car, especially an American one from the 1960s and 70s.

clue.text: Nothing to talk about? Fine

parts.note: nought, the letter that looks like zero

indicators.note: brought about means turned round, so the word for chattering faces the other way

parts.note: to yak is to chatter

explanation.surface: Someone shrugs that there is nothing worth discussing, so all is fine.
explanation.definitionFit: Okay and fine are synonyms for satisfactory or acceptable.

clue.text: Screen two thirds of sitcom

indicators.note: taking two thirds of something leaves out its final third

parts.note: Hi-de-Hi! was a BBC sitcom set in a 1950s holiday camp

explanation.surface: Showing only part of a TV comedy on a screen.
explanation.walkthrough: The six-letter title splits into thirds HI, DE, HI; drop the last to keep HIDE.
explanation.definitionFit: To screen something is to hide it from view, a verb synonym.

clue.text: Now then — my virtue is shaky

indicators.note: something shaky is unsteady, so these letters are knocked out of their order

parts.note: fourteen letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: Someone confesses that their moral resolve is wobbling.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Now then' sounds like a single interjection; 'Now' alone is the definition and 'then' starts the letters to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: This very minute is an emphatic way of saying at once, immediately, at the present moment.

clue.text: Middle of appendix given severe cut

indicators.note: the middle of a word is its central letters, here the two at the centre of an eight-letter word

parts.note: the two central letters of appendix
grave and severe both mean serious

explanation.surface: A patient's appendix needs a severe incision in the middle.
explanation.walkthrough: The surgical picture makes 'cut' look like an operation; it is the definition, meaning to carve.
explanation.definitionFit: To engrave is to cut letters or designs into a hard surface.

clue.text: Farm worker drinks kind of port

indicators.note: whoever drinks something takes it inside, so one word goes into the other

parts.note: a hand is a manual worker
a USB port is a computer socket

explanation.surface: A farm labourer drinks a type of fortified wine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Farm worker' reads as one phrase, but 'Farm' is the definition. Port suggests the wine; here it is a computer socket.
explanation.definitionFit: To husband land is an old verb sense meaning to till or cultivate it, as in husbandry.

clue.text: Pipe blown as letter's read out by Spooner

indicators.note: the Reverend Spooner famously swapped the opening sounds of words, so the starts of two words trade places

parts.note: as and when both mean at the time that
an epistle is a formal letter
the two words said together with their opening sounds traded

explanation.surface: A tin whistle is played while a letter is read aloud by the famous clergyman.
explanation.walkthrough: Say 'when epistle' with the opening sounds swapped: the P moves to the front and the WH to the second word, giving 'pen-e whistle'.
explanation.definitionFit: A penny whistle is a cheap metal pipe played by blowing, also called a tin whistle.

clue.text: Dance around soggy ground not acceptable

indicators.note: ground means crushed up, as coffee beans are, so these letters are broken into a new order
non-U means not acceptable in upper-class usage, so the letter standing for that class is removed

parts.note: eleven letters, one of which will be dropped

explanation.surface: Dancing about on waterlogged ground just won't do.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Soggy ground' looks like a phrase, but 'ground' is the anagram signal. U means upper-class or acceptable, so 'not acceptable' removes it.
explanation.definitionFit: The Gay Gordons is a lively Scottish country dance, often done at ceilidhs.

clue.text: Cutting through wound not covered in some places

indicators.note: something cutting through another runs into its middle, so one word sits inside the other

parts.note: a road that wound its way snaked
a tart remark is a cutting one

explanation.surface: A knife cutting through a wound left exposed in places.
explanation.walkthrough: Most solvers write in STARK first; this regional form has T, and 'in some places' flags the dialect. 'Wound' is the past tense of wind, not an injury.
explanation.definitionFit: Start-naked is a dialect form of stark-naked, meaning completely bare, with nothing covering the body.

clue.text: Lying, possibly natural but not right

indicators.note: but not means excluding, so a letter is left out

parts.note: an inbred quality is innate or natural
the abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: Someone lying, perhaps naturally, though not truthfully.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lying' suggests telling untruths; here it means lying down. 'Possibly' marks it as one example.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone in bed is typically lying down, so lying is an example of the state.

clue.text: Old trader's carts — not a change

indicators.note: not a means without the letter a, which is dropped from the word

parts.note: drays are low carts for heavy loads, such as brewers' barrels
to alter is to change

explanation.surface: An old trader's carts haven't been changed at all.
explanation.definitionFit: A drysalter was a historical dealer in dyes, chemicals, salted foods and similar dry goods.

clue.text: Sharp or blunt

explanation.walkthrough: Sharp and blunt look like opposites, but a trenchant critic is both incisive and outspoken.
explanation.definitionFit: Trenchant describes vigorous, incisive comment that is cutting yet also direct and unvarnished.

clue.text: Great big fish

parts.note: hunky means big and strong
the dory is a sea fish, as in John Dory

explanation.surface: An admiring exclamation at a huge catch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Great big' reads as one phrase, but 'Great' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Hunky-dory is informal for fine or excellent, so everything is great.

clue.text: Turn right round, and the queen's got it

indicators.note: turned round means facing the other way, so the letters are read backwards

parts.note: a go is a turn in a game
the abbreviation for right
Elizabeth Regina, the late Queen's cipher

explanation.surface: A driver turns round, and the Queen understands the manoeuvre.
explanation.definitionFit: Roger is the radio code word meaning message received and understood.

clue.text: Left again for NYE — lost touch

indicators.note: something lost has gone astray, so these letters wander out of order

parts.note: the abbreviation for left
eleven letters rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone left once more for New Year's Eve and fell out of contact.
explanation.walkthrough: NYE is New Year's Eve; 'lost touch' reads as one idiom, but 'touch' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To lay a finger on someone is to touch them, usually used in threats or denials.

clue.text: Wall Street character good on City floor

definitions.note: a punning definition: a lizard found on walls, sounding like Gordon Gekko of the film Wall Street

parts.note: the abbreviation for good
EC is the postcode area of the City of London
to floor an opponent is to knock them out

explanation.surface: The ruthless trader from the film Wall Street, a good man on the City trading floor.
explanation.walkthrough: Gordon Gekko is the film's financier, spelt with KK; the answer is the wall-climbing lizard, a 'character' at home on walls.
explanation.definitionFit: Geckos are lizards with sticky toe pads that let them run up walls, so they are characters found on walls.

clue.text: Bag endless grouse

indicators.note: without its end means the final letter is dropped

parts.note: to grouse or gripe is to complain

explanation.surface: Shooting a game bird, and bagging one without end.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bag' and 'grouse' suggest a shoot; grouse is a complaint here.
explanation.definitionFit: A grip is a travelling bag or holdall, an older word for luggage.

clue.text: Son could easily study

parts.note: the abbreviation for son
can means is able, as in 'I can do that'

explanation.surface: A son could study without much trouble.
explanation.definitionFit: To scan a document is to examine or study it closely.

clue.text: Filling for calamari — cottage cheese

indicators.note: a filling sits inside something, so the letters are found inside the following words

parts.note: found spanning the end of the first word and start of the second

explanation.surface: A recipe idea: stuff squid with cottage cheese.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cottage cheese' reads as one food, but 'cheese' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Ricotta is a soft, mild Italian whey cheese, often used as a filling.

clue.text: Show pawnbroker unfinished wood

indicators.note: unfinished means lacking its end, so the final letter goes

parts.note: uncle is old slang for a pawnbroker
oak is a kind of wood

explanation.surface: Showing a pawnbroker a half-made wooden item.
explanation.definitionFit: To uncloak is to remove a covering and so reveal or show something.

clue.text: Crack on slate in storeroom

indicators.note: in an across clue, one thing on another comes after it, so the word for crack is placed second

parts.note: to slate or pan is to criticise harshly
to have a crack at something is to try it

explanation.surface: A crack in the slate floor of a storeroom.
explanation.definitionFit: A pantry is a small room for storing food and kitchen supplies.

clue.text: We'll regularly put out boxes, free of pests

indicators.note: something that boxes another encloses it like a box

parts.note: to douse a fire is to put it out

indicators.note: regularly means at even intervals, so every other letter is kept

parts.note: second and fourth letters of the word

explanation.surface: We'll set out boxes in order to be rid of vermin.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe in We'll is ignored when taking every other letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Deloused means rid of lice, a kind of pest.
